sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
Apply a voltage \(V_D\) with the p side negative (reverse bias, \(V_D < 0\)). The applied voltage adds to the built-in step, so the junction must hold back a larger total potential \(\varphi_{bi} - V_D\). To support it, the depletion region widens and uncovers more ion charge on each side.

Because the potential is proportional to width squared for a fixed doping, the width grows as the **square root** of the total potential. The depletion charge per area grows the same way. Only a tiny leakage current flows, carried by the few minority carriers that wander into the field.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ X_d(V_D) = \sqrt{\frac{2\varepsilon_{si}(\varphi_{bi} - V_D)}{q}\left(\frac{1}{N_A} + \frac{1}{N_D}\right)} \]
\[ |Q_j| = q N_A x_p = q N_D x_n = \sqrt{2q\varepsilon_{si}(\varphi_{bi} - V_D)\frac{N_AN_D}{N_A + N_D}} \]
Reverse bias: \(V_D < 0\), so \(\varphi_{bi} - V_D > \varphi_{bi}\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
A junction has \(\varphi_{bi} = 0.7\ \mathrm{V}\) and zero-bias width \(0.3\ \mu\mathrm{m}\). At \(V_D = -6.3\ \mathrm{V}\) the total potential is \(7.0\ \mathrm{V}\), ten times larger:
\[ X_d = 0.3\ \mu\mathrm{m}\times\sqrt{10} \approx 0.95\ \mu\mathrm{m} \]
The width tripled, not grew tenfold.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Using \(V_D\) alone and forgetting \(\varphi_{bi}\).
- Adding magnitudes with the wrong sign convention (\(\varphi_{bi} + V_D\) with negative \(V_D\)).
- Assuming width scales linearly with voltage.
- Forgetting that both sides grow, in the inverse ratio of their dopings.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Because the depletion charge changes with reverse voltage, the junction acts as a voltage-dependent capacitor. That is the next skill, and it is how varactors and parasitic diode capacitances behave. Remember the square-root dependence; it is the reason varactors need several volts of swing to tune over a useful range.
